title: Globular cluster M 10
caption: The globular cluster Messier 10, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: M 10 · constellation Ophiuchus · about 15000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble view looks into the brightest part of the core of Messier 10, a globular cluster, which is a dense ball of stars. The region shown is about 13 light-years across.

Messier 10 owes its catalog name to Charles Messier, the 18th-century French astronomer who mainly hunted comets. Through the telescopes of his day, comets, nebulae, star clusters and galaxies all looked like faint, fuzzy blobs. What set them apart was motion. Comets drift slowly against the background stars, while the others stay put. Messier listed the fixed objects so they would not be mistaken for comets, and his list of just over 100 entries now includes many of the sky's best-known sights. Messier 10 appeared in the very first edition, published in 1774, which had 45 objects.

The cluster is roughly 80 light-years across, so in principle it should look about two thirds the size of the Moon. But its outskirts are extremely diffuse, and even its brighter core is too faint for the unaided eye.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.38 x 3.38 arcminutes) and distance (15000 light years), the frame spans roughly 15 × 15 light-years. Its light set out about 15,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared observations from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The cluster's core is too dim to see with the naked eye, and the near-infrared data are invisible to it. Hubble's long exposures reveal its individual stars.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.

explore: Messier 10 lies about 15 000 light-years away in Ophiuchus. The observations came from a large Hubble survey of the Milky Way's globular clusters. A contestant called flashenthunder entered a version of the image in Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition, which invited enthusiasts to search the archive.
alt: A dense field of stars from the bright core of a globular cluster.
